set.plain: Two studies by one team, one in south London and a larger one in 11 places in Europe and Brazil, compared people who had a first episode of psychosis with people from the same areas who had not. People with psychosis more often said they had used strong types of cannabis. In both studies the strongest link was with using strong types every day: about 5 times the odds of psychosis compared with never using. In the larger study, daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times the odds, and the gap between these two could be due to chance; in the London study, daily use of weaker types was not linked. In the larger study, using any type only now and then was not linked to psychosis; in the London study, using strong types less than once a week went with nearly 2 times the odds. In both studies, using weaker types was not linked once all patterns of use were counted together. Several numbers printed in the London study do not fit together. Nobody measured the strength of the cannabis people actually used: it was guessed from the type they named, after they became ill. These studies cannot show that strong cannabis caused the psychosis.
